In summary, our research is concerned with
developing a new class of algorithms for regulating the traffic in large, high performance switches and routers.
the design and analysis of algorithms for distributed queueing in high performance routers.
the design of scalable, high performance routers, and in particular with the problem of regulating the flow of packets through the router fabric.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
for the case of uniform random traffic, a distributed queueing algorithm is a very good choice for a high performance router, even if the router is not very large.
for uniform random input traffic, a speedup factor of 1.2 is enough to guarantee negligible loss of output link throughput due to sub-optimum rate allocation, even in a 64-port switch.
distributed queueing algorithms are a viable and attractive alternative for regulating the flow through large routers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the distributed queueing algorithms presented in this paper are able to achieve the throughput and delay performance that is expected for crossbar scheduling mechanisms, while at the same time, they are able to achieve a significant reduction in the amount of control traffic generated.

we have designed, simulated and implemented distributed queueing algorithms that are scalable to large router sizes and that are capable of providing high performance and low loss operation for a wide variety of traffic patterns and traffic mixes.
the distributed queueing algorithms presented in this paper are able to provide the same level of performance as crossbar-scheduling algorithms, with significantly less communication overhead.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a distributed algorithm can achieve the same performance as a centralized algorithm with only a modest increase in complexity.
the use of distributed algorithms for queue management in large high performance routers is feasible.
a simple and elegant distributed queueing scheme can be used to regulate the flow of traffic in large, high performance switches.
